selected_mechanism.name: The 10 U.S.C. 2922a purchase-approval gate on the Eielson micro-reactor
selected_mechanism.one_line_definition: A private developer would build, own and operate a 5-megawatt nuclear micro-reactor inside the fence at Eielson AFB and sell the base electricity and heat under a contract of up to 30 years, but the Air Force cannot buy that power until the Secretary of Defense personally approves the proposed contract, and it cannot clear the preferred site until a wetlands finding clears the service's own NEPA regulation.

news_trigger.verbatim_quote: The Air Force's preferred site is located near wetlands, so the agency must first ask for public comment on the project, as required by federal law.
news_trigger.secondary_verbatim_quote: Members of the public can offer comments, but they must be submitted to the Eielson Public Affairs Office no later than Sept. 30.

layers.layer_name: Wetlands siting gate — Air Force EIAP
layers.what_it_does: Because the preferred Spruce Lake parcel sits in or near wetlands, the Environmental Assessment and an UNSIGNED Finding of No Significant Impact must be public for at least 30 days before approval, and a Finding of No Practicable Alternative must be routed to the MAJCOM Environmental Planning Function. This is the regulation that produces the comment window now running.
layers.controlling_actor: Air Force Environmental Protection Committee (EPC), at the approval level determined by the MAJCOM — an institutional body, not a named officer

layers.layer_name: The substantive wetlands standard — EO 11990 Sec. 2(a)
layers.what_it_does: Supplies the actual legal test the FONPA must satisfy: no new construction in wetlands unless the agency head finds there is no practicable alternative AND that the action includes all practicable measures to minimize harm. Two prongs, one finding.
layers.controlling_actor: Head of the agency (Secretary of the Air Force), exercised through the EIAP delegation above

layers.what_it_does: Lets a service secretary contract for up to 30 years for the provision and operation of an energy production facility and the purchase of the energy it produces, with energy security and energy resilience mandated as critical factors. Subsection (b) conditions the entire authority on one external approval.
layers.controlling_actor: Secretary of the Air Force to propose; Secretary of Defense to approve under subsection (b)

layers.layer_name: Counterparty layer — the tentatively selected developer
layers.what_it_does: The reactor is commercially owned and operated; the government buys power, not a reactor. The selected developer's own SEC filing states the selection is not final and is conditioned on Air Force requirements, meaning no executed power purchase agreement exists.
layers.controlling_actor: Oklo Inc. (CIK 0001849056), as the tentatively selected developer — the role, not the officeholder

chokepoint.binary_decision: Approve the proposed long-term energy purchase contract, or do not. Without that approval no contract may be made at all.
chokepoint.why_asymmetric: The statute is unconditional and singular: 'A contract may be made under subsection (a) only after the approval of the proposed contract by the Secretary of Defense.' No vote, no board, no protest path, no delegation named in the text. Compare the two chokepoints the scouts proposed: the FONSI/FONPA is approved by the Environmental Protection Committee at a MAJCOM-determined level (32 CFR 989.15), a committee, and no primary source names a signer; and the NRC framing rests on a docket that does not exist for this site. 2922a(b) is the only layer in the chain where one officer owns a genuinely binary, statutorily mandatory yes/no.
chokepoint.verbatim_statutory_span: A contract may be made under subsection (a) only after the approval of the proposed contract by the Secretary of Defense.

selected_mechanism.ak_consequence: Interior Alaska power and compute siting: any developer, utility planner or allocator underwriting behind-the-fence firm generation at Eielson before 2030 is pricing a contract that does not yet exist. Oklo Inc.'s own FY2025 10-K says it has been 'tentatively selected' and that this 'has not been finalized,' and under 10 U.S.C. 2922a(b) no purchase contract can be made at all until the Secretary of Defense approves it. The nearest public input point on the site itself closes 2026-09-30.
selected_mechanism.structural_read: The story in the window is a wetlands comment period, and the wetlands gate is real. It is what sets the September 30 clock and it is the only point where an outside party gets a channel. But it is not where the leverage sits. The Air Force's own regulation routes the finding to a committee and lets the MAJCOM pick the approval level, which is exactly the shape of a process designed to be survivable. The hard gate is upstream of the concrete: a thirty-year obligation to buy power from a privately owned reactor cannot be made without a single signature at the top of the Department. That is why the developer's SEC filing uses the word 'tentatively' in both the business section and the risk factors. The project is being narrated locally as an environmental review and structurally as an acquisition, and the acquisition is the part that has not happened.
selected_mechanism.forward_implication: If you are modeling Interior Alaska firm power, a Fairbanks-area load, a Railbelt interconnection, or any siting decision that assumes Eielson gets 5 MW of behind-the-fence generation by 2030, do not carry it as contracted capacity this week. Carry it as an option contingent on a Secretary of Defense approval that has no public docket and no deadline, and build the case on the existing Interior grid. If you want the wetlands record to reflect your interest, the comment channel to Eielson Public Affairs closes 2026-09-30.
selected_mechanism.recurrence_note: Not on the burned list. The chain here is federal energy-purchase authority (10 U.S.C. 2922a) plus EO 11990, which is legally distinct from every previously anatomized mechanism, including the Anchorage AMC Title 21 CUP gate, FPA 4(f) site-banking, and the AS 38.05.810 conveyance. The facilities scout's explicit repeat-risk flag ('third siting-adjacent piece in eight issues') attached to the 10 U.S.C. 2667 Enhanced Use Lease framing, which was NOT selected. Selecting the contract-approval framing over the siting framing also reduces that adjacency.

overlap_adjudication: Candidate A surfaced from both the facilities and regulatory scouts on the same KUAC trigger, with competing chokepoint reads. Three candidate chokepoints were tested against the asymmetry point and both scout framings failed. (1) NRC licensing, the facilities read: fails per-layer sourcing — no Eielson-specific docket exists, the NRC page never names Eielson, and the Aurora is listed at 75 MWe against a 5 MW reported unit. (2) The EO 11990 Sec. 2(a) FONPA, the regulatory read: 32 CFR 989.15 fetched directly resolves the weak link the scout flagged — 'The same organizational level that prepares the EA also reviews and recommends the FONSI for approval by the EPC,' with MAJCOMs determining the approval level. A committee at a variable level; 989.14(g) adds only that the FONPA is submitted to the MAJCOM EPF. No primary source names a signer. Fails asymmetry. (3) The 10 U.S.C. 2922a(b) Secretary of Defense approval, which neither scout selected: verified verbatim on uscode.house.gov and corroborated on Cornell LII. One officer, statutorily mandatory, unconditional, binary, with no committee and no delegation in the text. Per the overlap rule, leverage decides, so the third framing wins. This also shifts the category from the scouts' facilities/regulatory to vehicles, because the chokepoint sits in the acquisition layer rather than the siting layer, a side benefit given the burned list is siting-heavy. The wetlands gate is retained as Layer 1, where it is accurate and where it carries the live September 30 date.
